Connect to foundations: Stellar structure and the mass–luminosity relation ↗ Compare solution assumptions and boundary data in the solution library ↗ 01When does a blast wave become simple? Deposit energy E in a small region of a uniform gas of density ρ₀. A spherical blast expands into initially stationary material with negligible upstream pressure compared with the shock pressure. Use an ideal gas with constant heat-capacity ratio γ, neglecting gravity, magnetic forces, and radiative cooling. For a supernova remnant this model mainly applies after the swept-up mass dominates the ejecta and before radiative losses become important. It does not describe the instant of explosion or the later radiative shell stage. 02Obtain the two-fifths exponent from units Write the shock radius as R = C Eᵃρ₀ᵇtᶜ. Since [E] = ML²T⁻² and [ρ₀] = ML⁻³, matching mass, length, and time gives three linear equations for the exponents. a+b = 0, 2a−3b = 1, −2a+c = 0 a = 15, b = −15, c = 25 R = β(Et²ρ₀)1/5, D ≡ dRdt = 2R5t Call the dimensionless coefficient β. The energy estimate E ∼ ρ₀R³D² gives the same exponents, but dimensional analysis cannot determine β. We must solve the interior and normalize its total energy. 03Derive the Rankine–Hugoniot conditions In the shock frame, label upstream and downstream states 1 and 2. Let positive w₁ and w₂ be their speeds through the front. Across a thin, steady front, mass, momentum, and energy fluxes per unit area must match. ρ₁w₁ = ρ₂w₂ p₁+ρ₁w₁² = p₂+ρ₂w₂² w₁²2 + γp₁(γ−1)ρ₁ = w₂²2 + γp₂(γ−1)ρ₂ The last equation is energy flux divided by the common mass flux. Pressure work adds to internal energy to give the specific enthalpy γp/[(γ−1)ρ]. Set χ = ρ₂/ρ₁, so w₂ = w₁/χ. Momentum conservation gives p₂ = p₁ + ρ₁w₁²(1−1/χ). Substitute both into the energy equation and remove the unchanged-flow root χ = 1 to obtain the compressive solution. χ = (γ+1)ℳ₁²(γ−1)ℳ₁²+2, ℳ₁² ≡ ρ₁w₁²γp₁ For a strong shock, ℳ₁ ≫ 1, χ tends to (γ+1)/(γ−1). With stationary upstream gas, w₁ = D and the downstream laboratory speed is u₂ = D − w₂. A monatomic gas with γ = 5/3 gives χ = 4, u₂ = 3D/4, and p₂ = 3ρ₀D²/4. The factor four is the strong-shock limit for an adiabatic monatomic gas converting bulk kinetic energy to heat. Entropy increases across the front; the smooth-flow entropy equation below must not be applied through the discontinuity. 04Combine time and radius into one variable Let u be outward fluid velocity, p pressure, and ρ density. In the smooth interior, spherical mass conservation, momentum balance, and adiabatic evolution hold. A partial derivative ∂ varies one coordinate while holding the other fixed. ∂ρ∂t + 1r²∂∂r(r²ρu) = 0 ∂u∂t + u∂u∂r = −1ρ∂p∂r (∂∂t+u∂∂r) (pργ) = 0 Set x = r/R and scale density by ρ₀, velocity by D, and pressure by ρ₀D². Seek profiles G, V, and Z depending only on x. ρ = ρ₀G(x), u = DV(x), p = ρ₀D²Z(x) ∂x∂r = 1R, ∂x∂t = −DRx For example, ∂ρ/∂t = −ρ₀(D/R)xG′, while the mass-flux derivative is ρ₀(D/R)(G′V + GV′ + 2GV/x). Cancelling the common factor gives the first equation below. 05Similarity ODEs and shock boundaries R ∝ t2/5 implies R(dD/dt)/D² = −3/2. Apply the same chain rule to momentum and adiabatic evolution to reduce the PDEs to three ODEs. Primes now denote x derivatives. (V−x)G′ + G(V′+2V/x) = 0 (V−x)V′ − 32V = −Z′G (V−x)(Z′Z−γG′G) = 3 The shock is at x = 1. Nondimensionalizing the jump conditions supplies the starting values. G(1) = γ+1γ−1, V(1) = 2γ+1, Z(1) = 2γ+1 For γ = 5/3 integrate inward from (4, 3/4, 3/4). The physical branch approaches V → 0, G → 0, and finite Z at the centre. Low density can coexist with finite pressure, unlike a uniformly filled expanding sphere. 06Normalize the total energy to determine β Total energy is kinetic plus internal energy. Their densities are ρu²/2 and p/(γ−1); integrate using the volume element 4πr²dr. I ≡ ∫01 [GV²2+Zγ−1]x²dx E = 4πρ₀R³D²I = 16π25ρ₀R⁵t²I β = (2516πI)1/5 ≈ 1.15167 (γ = 5/3) The panel integrates at fixed γ = 5/3 from x = 1 to 0.05 using Runge–Kutta, evolving logarithms of G and Z to preserve positivity. It approximates the small central thermal-energy contribution with constant Z(0.05); profiles below x = 0.05 are not plotted. The displayed β is a numerical estimate. 07Use conservation laws to challenge the solution The enclosed mass should equal the initially swept volume times density, 4πρ₀R³/3. Thus 3∫Gx²dx = 1 is an independent check. Refine the step and verify convergence of the mass ratio and β. Radius and shock speed imply t = 2R/(5D). With density as well, infer E = ρ₀R⁵/(β⁵t²). Observed gas velocity is not generally the shock-front speed D. Cosmic-ray pressure, particle escape, or a nonuniform medium can change these ideal-gas coefficients and compression ratios. The next chapter begins with acceleration in the limit where energetic particles do not modify the flow. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. At the same ambient density and elapsed time, how do radius and speed change if the energy increases by 32? Given a measured shock radius R and shock speed D, what is the model age? Show the answer and reasoning Both R and D scale as E1/5, so both double. Since D = 2R/(5t), the model age is t = 2R/(5D). Using R/D ignores deceleration and overestimates the age by a factor of 5/2. This applies only to an energy-conserving, spherical strong shock in a uniform medium. REFERENCES & PHYSICAL INPUTS Explanations and derivations are written for this guide. References may use different notation or normalization. Panel methods and approximations are stated in the text.
